items.headline: Voyager 1 reaches one light‑day distance from Earth after 49 years
items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
items.scifi_hook: The 1977 probe finally sent a signal from a distance equal to a full day of light travel.
items.eli5: Voyager 1 is now 16.1 billion miles away, the farthest any human‑made object has traveled.
items.why: It demonstrates the durability of deep‑space probes and informs future interstellar missions.
items.text: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday. “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.” Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. items.headline: New cryptography‑based method speeds pulsar discovery in Fermi data
items.title: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars
items.scifi_hook: Scientists can now spot hidden spinning neutron stars a million times faster using public gamma‑ray data.
items.eli5: A new computer trick lets researchers find pulsars in NASA data in hours instead of centuries.
items.why: Accelerated pulsar detection expands our knowledge of extreme astrophysical objects.
items.text: 5 min read NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, illustrated here, scans the entire sky every three hours as it orbits Earth. Its publicly available data helps scientists find the rapidly spinning cores of dead stars, known as pulsars. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/Chris Smith (USRA/GESTAR) An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters. Using 15 years of data from NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor. By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation. A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. items.why: Engine testing reduces risk and improves performance for upcoming crewed Moon launches.

NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Nov. 18 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for the planned duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds). While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability for future Artemis missions. items.headline: Ivanhoe Electric reports high‑grade copper‑gold‑silver find in Arizona
items.title: Friedland’s Ivanhoe Electric strikes high-grade copper in Arizona
items.scifi_hook: A drill hole in the desert uncovered a massive vein of copper, gold and silver.
items.eli5: The company hit a long section of rock with nearly 1% copper and valuable gold and silver inside.
items.why: The discovery could boost domestic copper supply and support U.S. metal demand.
items.text: Ivanhoe Electric (NYSE American: IE; TSX: IE), backed by mining billionaire Robert Friedland, has discovered high-grade copper-gold-silver mineralization at its Gleeson project in southeastern Arizona, making it the company’s top exploration priority. The company reporte d Thursday that drilling identified two mineralized zones, including 123.6 metres grading 0.91% copper, 0.44 gram of gold per tonne and 5.27 grams of silver per tonne from a depth of 601.7 metres. The interval included 71.03 metres grading 1.38% copper, 0.52 gram of gold and 6.73 grams of silver. “These initial drill results are some of the best copper-gold-silver intercepts drilled in the Western United States in the last ten years,” executive chairman Friedland and president and CEO Taylor Melvin said in a joint statement. The discovery, 28 miles north of Arizona’s historic Bisbee mining district, could provide another growth opportunity alongside Ivanhoe Electric’s Santa Cruz Copper Project near Casa Grande, where it plans to produce refined copper domestically. The results come as copper prices plunged about 6% this week to $12,471 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange, their lowest since April. Investors have been unwinding bets on artificial intelligence-driven demand and potential US tariffs on refined copper, with the sell-off accelerating after billionaire investor Stan Druckenmiller turned bearish . items.headline: Researchers achieve 99% pure cerium orthoferrite via hydrogen reduction
items.title: Successful high-purity synthesis of the challenging-to-produce cerium orthoferrite!
items.scifi_hook: Scientists crack a stubborn crystal recipe, unlocking ultra‑pure magnetic material.
items.eli5: By fine‑tuning hydrogen gas, they made a nearly perfect mix of cerium and iron oxide.
items.why: Pure cerium orthoferrite can improve magnetic devices and catalytic processes.
items.text: A research team including scientists from Ehime University successfully synthesized high-purity CeFeO3, a difficult-to-produce cerium–iron mixed oxide, using hydrogen reduction. By optimizing hydrogen concentration and gas flow rate, they achieved a phase purity of up to 99 mol%. The team also clarified the formation mechanism and identified factors that hinder synthesis. This method, published in the journal Inorganic Chemistry, provides a foundation for future research into applications in magnetic materials and catalysis.
